label: GPT-6 Astra
output:
Dear Kelechi,

You said I should put it in writing, so here we are. An actual letter, sent through the post to Croydon. Please appreciate the effort. Apparently, after all these years of friendship, my voice notes are no longer sufficient and you now require formal correspondence.

I am writing to ask you to come with me to the teacher-training open evening in Lewisham on Thursday 19 November, at 6pm. That is the request. Not resign from your job. Not buy a whistle and start shouting at children. Just come and hear what they have to say.

At my birthday, when you started again about your job and how every day is the same spreadsheet, I teased you. Obviously. You cannot come and eat birthday food and turn the occasion into a quarterly review of your suffering. But I was listening. You have been at that firm for nine years, and lately, whenever we talk about work, you sound tired in a way that a weekend does not seem to fix.

I don’t think teaching is a cure for every kind of dissatisfaction. Some days it supplies fresh dissatisfaction of its own. But when I said you should come and teach maths, I wasn’t just finding something to say between mouthfuls. I meant it, and not simply because you got an A in Further Maths, although you have certainly allowed us to remember that achievement.

I have seen you teach.

You were tutoring half our hostel in Moremi before exams. People came to you confused and slightly ashamed that they were confused, and somehow you got them asking questions. You could explain the same thing three different ways without making the person feel that the problem was their intelligence. That matters more than you think. Plenty of people know maths. Some of them should never be allowed to explain it to anybody.

Then there was my nephew at Christmas. We were supposed to be eating, and you turned plates of jollof into a fractions lesson. He still talks about it. You noticed what he wasn’t getting, found something he understood, and worked from there. No big announcement about how you were about to educate the youth. Just you, some rice, and patience.

That is why I am bothering you. Not because I think every bored quantity surveyor should be sent into a classroom.

You are patient. You are funny. You explain things without making people feel stupid. Children notice that last one very quickly. By secondary school, some have already decided that maths is a room they are not allowed into. They sit down expecting to fail, and sometimes they would rather cause trouble than let anyone see them trying. A teacher who can get them to risk an answer has something valuable.

Last month, I spent three weeks trying to get simultaneous equations to click for Damola, one of my Year 11 boys. Three weeks of examples, wrong turns, and me wondering what else I could possibly draw or say. Then he got it. He looked at his work and shouted, “Is that all??” as if I had personally been hiding the simplicity of it from him. The whole class clapped.

I wish you had been there. You would have laughed at his face.

I went home happy that day. Not because everything else had gone brilliantly, but because one boy who thought he couldn’t do something now knew he could. Those moments are part of why I stay.

Now, before you accuse me of sending you a recruitment brochure with a stamp on it, let me tell you the other part.

When I started in 2019, I cried in the car park twice in my first term. Twice that I am admitting to in a document you can keep. I was overwhelmed, tired, and not nearly as good at the job as I wanted to be. Knowing the maths and getting a room full of children to learn it are different things. There were lessons I planned carefully that went badly, and evenings when I was still thinking about something I should have handled differently.

It got better. I learned, I asked for help, and I stopped treating every difficult lesson as evidence that I had chosen the wrong life. But it was hard, and it still is.

The marking can feel endless. Behaviour some days is proper wahala. You can explain an instruction clearly, repeat it, put it on the board, and still hear, “What are we doing?” There is work outside school hours. The holidays are a real benefit, yes, but I am not going to pretend every day of them is spent with my feet up. If what you want is an easier job, I cannot honestly promise you this one.

I also know the money matters. You would be taking a pay drop in the first year, and enthusiasm does not pay bills in Croydon any more than it does in Peckham. The route I want you to look at is the salaried one: you get paid while you train, it takes a year, and the start would be September 2027. Salaried does not mean the drop suddenly becomes painless. We need to hear the actual figures and you need to do your sums.

There is the pension, there are the holidays, and pay goes up as you progress. All worth considering, none a reason to wave away the first-year difference. You are the quantity surveyor. Bring your questions about money. For once, I am actively encouraging the spreadsheet.

And please don’t tell me you are too old. You are 34, Kelechi. A woman in my department started at 41. You would have things to learn, certainly, but you would not be arriving empty-handed. Nine years of working with numbers, dealing with people, and being responsible for getting things right count for something.

Our school has about 1,100 children, and two Year 9 maths groups have had supply cover since September. I mention that because the need is real, not because those children are now your personal responsibility. You don’t owe anybody a career change. I just think you could be good at this, and I would like you to see what the route looks like before dismissing it.

On your last birthday, you said, “I just want to do something that matters before 40.”

I remember. I am not going to use it to deliver a sermon. Your work now matters too, and checking other people’s costings is skilled work, even if I enjoy insulting it. But I do wonder whether it gives enough room to the parts of you I have known since Unilag. The patience. The humour. The satisfaction you get when somebody finally understands.

So come on the 19th. Thursday, 6pm, Lewisham. Applications for next September open soon, and this is a chance to ask awkward questions before making any decisions. Ask about the salary, the workload, the support when things go wrong, and what a training week actually involves. I will come with you.

You can leave afterwards and say, “Absolutely not.” I will accept that. I may still tease you about your spreadsheet, but that arrangement predates this letter.

No signing your life away. No resignation letter on Monday morning. Just one evening to find out whether an idea we laughed about at my birthday might be worth taking seriously.

Message me when this arrives, so I know Royal Mail has completed its part in your career development. Then tell me you’re coming.

Your friend,

The person who has now put it in writing
